# Block 8: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged {.unnumbered} You let an agent turn working code into a function and prove that nothing changed. The proof is a characterisation testA test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct., as in the [tidy-evaluation chapter](05-tidy-evaluation.qmd): the new code must reproduce the original output exactly. That output is frozen as a referenceIn a characterisation test, the saved output of the original, trusted code (stored in tests/fixtures/). A trusted script captures it once, from the unchanged code, before any refactoring, and you commit it. After that, nothing regenerates it except your own recorded decision.. Then you decide whether the unchanged output is right. Changing it on purpose, and recording why, is an exercise for after the day. *⏱ ~25 minutes · Start on `main` (or `checkpoint-cleaning`), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.* :::{#block8-files .callout-note collapse="true"} ## This block's files, and how it fits This block goes back to `data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv`, the data you explored in Block 3, not Block 7's cleaned file. Block 7's tests run with everything else, and skip if you did not finish Block 7. Nothing needs downloading. Short of time at any step? `checkpoint-refactor` has Step 1 done. The block follows [the safe vibe-coding recipe](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd#safe-recipe): your part is one request, one commit, one read of the diff and one test run. | File | Written by | Its job | Step | |---|---|---|---| | `scripts/05_analysis.R`, `scripts/04_load_data.R`, `scripts/functions/load_voles.R` | Course team | The original, trusted analysis you will refactor, and the loading it relies on | 1 | | `tests/make_reference.R` | Course team | The capture script: saves the original output as the reference | 1, 2 | | Deny rules `Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)` and `Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)` | Course team (you met them in Block 5) | Keep the agent's edit tools off the reference and its capture script | 0 | | `.agents/skills/characterisation-refactor/` (and its copy in `.claude/skills/`) | Course team | The procedure: capture, refactor, test, in that order | 1 | | `tests/test_reference_guard.R`, `tests/test_controls.R` | Course team | Check that the agent's test reads your reference file and calls the function, that the reference is unchanged since your commit, and that the new test is protected | 1, 2 | | `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds` | The skill runs `make_reference.R`; **you** commit it | The reference | 1 | | `scripts/functions/summary_functions.R`, `tests/test_summary_functions.R`; changes to `05_analysis.R` | The agent | The refactor and its characterisation test | 1 | | `Edit(/tests/test_summary_functions.R)` in `.claude/settings.json` | You, with `/permissions` | Protects the new test | 1 | | `tests/test_known_answers.R`; changes to `summary_functions.R`; the re-captured reference | The agent; you re-capture | The intended change, tested | 2 (after the day) | | A line in `docs/ai-log.md` | You | The record of AI use | 1 (and 2, after the day) | ::: ## Step 0: check the protections {#step-0} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Recipe check (3 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** confirm the reference and its capture script are protected, and that no reference exists yet, so that the reference you capture in Step 1 can only come from the original code. **Start state:** as at the top of the page. **1. Check the protections.** In Claude Code, type `/permissions`. The deny rulesA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. `Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)` and `Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)` keep the agent's edit tools off the reference and its capture script. The Git pane shows a change made by any other route. **2. Check there is no reference yet.** In the Files pane, open `tests/fixtures/`. It should hold only `raw_checksum.txt` (Block 7). **You are done when** you have seen the two rules, and `tests/fixtures/` has no `.rds` file. **If it goes wrong:** far behind? Switch to `checkpoint-refactor` in the Git pane's branch menu and read on. :::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The shipped capture script, `tests/make_reference.R` It runs the original `05_analysis.R` and saves the result. The course team wrote it; a deny rule stops the agent editing it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/make_reference.R ---- # Run ONCE, by you, BEFORE any refactoring. source(here::here("scripts", "05_analysis.R")) dir.create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE) saveRDS( metabolic_summary, here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds") ) ``` ::: ::: ::::::::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How the pieces fit ::::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="The characterisation-test loop. Step 1, refactor without changing the output: the skill runs your shipped make_reference.R on the original code; you commit the reference; the skill refactors only; you read the diff; the skill writes a test that reads your reference and runs only that test; you protect the new test with /permissions; you restart R and the whole test suite passes. Step 2, when the behaviour should change: you decide the output is wrong; the agent changes the function; the characterisation test fails, correctly; the known-answer test passes; you re-capture, with a commit message saying why. Nothing regenerates the reference once you have committed it, except your own recorded decision."} :::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Step 1: refactor without changing the output ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Skill: run `make_reference.R` on the original code ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Commit the reference ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Skill: refactor only ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Read the diff ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Skill: a test that reads your reference, run on its own ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Protect the new test (`/permissions`) ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Restart R: the whole test suite passes ::: :::::: :::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Step 2: when the behaviour should change ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Decide the output is wrong ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Change the function ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Characterisation test fails, correctly ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Known-answer test passes ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Re-capture, with a commit message saying why ::: :::::: ::: {.dia-caption} A reference made after the code changed is produced by the code under test, and can only confirm that the code agrees with itself. Committing it first is what makes it a reference. ::: ::::::: :::::::: ## Step 1: snapshot, refactor and test with the skill {#step-1} `scripts/05_analysis.R` summarises post-treatment metabolic rate (mean, SD and count) by treatment arm and sex. Notice one thing and leave it alone. One animal has no `metabolic_rate_post`, and the code has no `na.rm`, so the mean and the SD for its group are both `NA`. The shipped skillA reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description. `characterisation-refactor` does the work in order and stops for you after each part. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Reference: the code you will refactor, and the loading it relies on ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/05_analysis.R: the original, trusted version ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "04_load_data.R")) metabolic_summary <- voles |> group_by(treatment_arm, sex) |> summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = n(), .groups = "drop" ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/04_load_data.R ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) voles <- load_voles() ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/load_voles.R ---- load_voles <- function() { readr::read_csv( here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"), col_types = readr::cols( subject_id = readr::col_character(), sex = readr::col_character(), treatment_arm = readr::col_character(), mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(), mass_post_g = readr::col_double(), metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double() ) ) } ``` ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} One request, one commit, one diff, one test run (20 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** one request to the skill, ending with a committed reference, a refactored function and a protected test that proves the output unchanged, so that you can restructure working code without fearing that its results moved. **Start state:** Step 0 done, Git pane clean. In Claude Code, type `/clear` to clear any earlier conversation. **1. Ask.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /characterisation-refactor Move the summary in scripts/05_analysis.R into summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R. ``` The skill shows its plan as a message and waits. Read it: the plan should capture the reference first. Then reply in Claude Code: *Yes, go ahead*, or say what to change. **2. Approve the capture, then commit the reference.** The skill asks to run `tests/make_reference.R`. **Answer each request with plain Yes or No.** Never choose an option that says *don't ask again*: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now. Refusing is always safe. Here you can say both: it saves the original code's output before anything changes. When the skill stops, the Git pane should show only `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds` as new. Commit it ("Capture reference output before refactoring"), then tell the agent to carry on. **3. Read the diff when it stops again.** In the Git pane, click **Diff** on each changed file. Look for anything beyond moving the code into the function. Then tell the agent to carry on and write the test. If it asks whether to commit the refactor first, reply *No, go ahead*: you commit everything at the end. **4. Protect the new test.** The skill runs only its new test file, reports the output and stops. Now protect that test, so the agent cannot later change it to make a failing run pass. In `/permissions`, add the deny rule `Edit(/tests/test_summary_functions.R)`. Save it to the project's shared settings file, `.claude/settings.json`. **5. Run the whole suite.** Restart R (*Session → Restart R*), so that nothing left in your session can make a test pass. Then run this in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests")) ``` ::: | Test | Passing proves | |---|---| | `test_summary_functions.R` (the agent's) | the function reproduces your reference exactly | | `test_reference_guard.R` (shipped) | the agent's test reads your reference file and calls the function, and the reference is unchanged since your commit | | `test_controls.R` (shipped) | every deny rule is in place, including your new one | The guard cannot tell whether numbers were also typed into the test. Reading the test can. Other blocks' tests pass or skip. **6. Record it.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` (date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed): ask the agent to draft it, as in Block 3, then write the last part yourself. Note whether the test passed first time. **You are done when** the suite has no failures and the Git pane shows only the function, `05_analysis.R`, the new test, `.claude/settings.json` and your log as changed. Commit them. **If it goes wrong:** see *Fixes for Step 1* below the task, or switch to `checkpoint-refactor`. **Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again? :::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Fixes for Step 1 - **The capture.** If the agent declines to run `make_reference.R`, or a guard hook from Block 5 blocks it, capture the reference yourself. Restart R, run `source(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R"))`, commit the `.rds`, and tell the agent the reference is committed. - **Changed files.** If anything other than the `.rds` changed before your commit, **Revert** it in the Git pane and ask again. The Git pane undoes a change whatever made it; `/rewind` undoes only changes made with the agent's edit tools, not by R code it ran ([Block 5](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)). - **Row order.** If the test fails on row order, not values, the function used `.by` without sorting. Ask the agent to add `dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)`. - **The new rule.** If `test_controls.R` says the test is unprotected, check the rule's spelling in `/permissions`. If `settings.json` is not in the Git pane, the rule went to the local file: remove it there and add it again, choosing `.claude/settings.json`. If the agent offers to add the rule itself, refuse: it is yours to add. Otherwise, **Revert** the agent's files and ask again, or switch to `checkpoint-refactor`. ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How it works: the capture, the settings file and the test rules **The capture.** The skill runs `make_reference.R` only if no reference exists yet and `scripts/` has no uncommitted changes. It never runs it again after that. Who runs the capture script matters less than *when*: before any code changes, from a script you trust, and committed by you. After that, git and `test_reference_guard.R` notice any change to the reference. **The shared settings file.** `/permissions` can save a rule to `.claude/settings.json`, which you commit. It can also save it to the local `.claude/settings.local.json`, which git ignores, so a rule saved there never reaches a commit. The rule takes effect at once. **No known-answer case yet.** Your `AGENTS.md` asks for a known-answer test with every new function. The skill's test rules take priority here. A characterisation test compares with the original output; known-answer tests come in Step 2, once you decide the behaviour should change. The skill also leaves the whole suite and the settings to you. ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## What the skill tells the agent (`characterisation-refactor/SKILL.md`) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` markdown --- name: characterisation-refactor description: >- Refactors working R analysis code into documented functions under a characterisation test, so the output is proved unchanged. Use when asked to functionalise, refactor or tidy a script whose output must not change. Not for fixing bugs or changing results. disable-model-invocation: true --- # Refactor under a characterisation test ## The reference comes from the original code, and the user commits it The frozen reference in tests/fixtures/ is written by the user's own capture script (tests/make_reference.R) from the original, unchanged code, and the user commits it before anything else changes. A reference made after the code has changed proves nothing. - Run tests/make_reference.R at most once, in step 2 below, and only if no reference exists yet and git status shows no uncommitted changes under scripts/. Never run it at any other time, and never edit the capture script. - Never edit, regenerate or delete anything under tests/fixtures/. - If a reference already exists, use it as it is. ## Procedure 1. Present a plan: whether a reference must be captured, the code to move, the function name and file, and the test file. Wait for the user to confirm. 2. Capture only, if no reference exists. Run git status; if anything under scripts/ has uncommitted changes, stop and ask. Otherwise run Rscript tests/make_reference.R, report the file it wrote, and stop: ask the user to commit it before you change any code. Do not commit it yourself. 3. Refactor only. Write the function in scripts/functions/ with a roxygen2 block and an argument check, and make the original script call it. Do not write or edit tests in this step. Stop and let the user review the diff. 4. Test only. Write tests/test_.R (for scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, that is tests/test_summary_functions.R). Start it with library(testthat) and testthat::local_edition(3), source the function files with here::here(), read the reference from tests/fixtures/ with readRDS(), and compare it with the function's output using expect_equal(). Never hard-code expected values, and never reimplement the computation inside the test. Include an expect_error() test showing that the argument check rejects data with a required column missing. This step's rules take precedence over any project instruction to add known-answer tests: those come later, if the user decides the behaviour should change. 5. Run only the new test file in a fresh R session, for example Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_summary_functions.R')", and report the output verbatim. Then stop: the user protects the new test and runs the whole suite. Do not change any settings file. ## Rules - If the test fails, report the difference. Never change the test, the tolerance or the reference to make it pass. - Sort the output rows explicitly with dplyr::arrange() on the grouping columns, so the order never depends on how the data happen to be stored. - Do not change behaviour, including how missing values are handled. A passing test shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct; list anything that looks wrong for the user to decide. ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using another tool **Posit Assistant.** It reads the same skill from `.agents/skills/`. Use it in Normal mode and run the same test suite. Posit Assistant has no path rules for edits, so the Git pane and `test_reference_guard.R` are what protect the reference. ::: ## Step 2: unchanged is not correct {#step-2} Your test passes, **including the `NA` mean and SD** for one group. If you wanted the mean of the animals that were measured, the original code was wrong all along. A characterisation test cannot tell: it compares against the past, not against the truth. Deciding whether the behaviour is correct is a separate step, and it is yours. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Discuss: is the original right? (3 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** decide whether the output you just protected is correct, so that you never mistake "unchanged" for "right". **1. Look at the reference.** In the R console, run `readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds"))`. One group's mean and SD are `NA`, and its `n` counts an animal that was never measured. **2. Answer in the chat:** is that what the analysis should report? If not, what would you change? And how would you prove the new behaviour is right, when the characterisation test will now fail by design?
Use measured animals only: `na.rm = TRUE` for the mean and SD, and a count of measured and missing animals instead of `n`. Prove it with a known-answer testA test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged.: a small table whose answer you work out by hand. Then re-capture the reference yourself, and commit it with a message saying why. The re-captured reference is a decision you recorded, not drift.
**You are done when** you can say why the passing test does not show the output is correct, and what would. :::: ::: ::::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Do it yourself (after the day): change the behaviour and re-capture :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Decide, change, and test the change independently (12 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** change the behaviour on purpose, prove it with a known-answer test, and record why the reference changed, so that anyone reading the history sees a decision, not drift. **1. Decide.** The mean and standard deviation should use measured animals only, and the count should not include the unmeasured animal (`n()` counts rows). **2. Ask for the change and a known-answer test.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text In summarise_metabolic_rate(), compute the mean and SD with na.rm = TRUE, and report n_used and n_missing instead of n. Add a known-answer test on a small tibble in a new file, tests/test_known_answers.R, and show me how you worked out the expected values. Do not change tests/test_summary_functions.R. ``` A known-answer testA test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged. checks the new behaviour against a result you can work out by hand. **Check the arithmetic yourself**: the mean of 10, 14 and a missing value is 12, from two measured animals.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: missing values handled ---- summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { stopifnot(is.data.frame(data)) required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post") missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data)) if (length(missing_cols) > 0) { stop( "`data` is missing required column(s): ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE ) } data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE), n_used = sum(!is.na(metabolic_rate_post)), n_missing = sum(is.na(metabolic_rate_post)), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) |> dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_known_answers.R ---- library(testthat) testthat::local_edition(3) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R")) test_that("means ignore missing values and n_used counts measured animals", { toy_df <- tibble::tibble( treatment_arm = c("Control", "Control", "Control"), sex = c("F", "F", "F"), metabolic_rate_post = c(10, 14, NA) ) result <- summarise_metabolic_rate(toy_df) expect_equal(result$mean_rate, 12) expect_equal(result$n_used, 2) expect_equal(result$n_missing, 1) }) ``` :::
**3. Watch the characterisation test fail, correctly.** Run the suite as in Step 1. The output has changed, so the characterisation test fails; the known-answer test passes. If the agent asks to run `make_reference.R`, refuse: re-capturing is your decision. **4. Re-capture the reference, as a recorded decision.** Restart R, then run this in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R")) ``` ::: **5. Commit, then run the suite.** Commit the reference, the function and the new test file. Use a message that says why, for example "Exclude missing metabolic rates from mean and SD; report n_used and n_missing". Only then run the suite as in Step 1: `test_reference_guard.R` fails while the new reference is uncommitted. Re-capturing is safe here for three reasons: you decided it, a known-answer test checks the new behaviour, and the commit records why. **6. Record it.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` (date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed) and commit it. **You are done when** the whole suite passes again, the re-captured reference is committed with its reason, and your AI-log line is committed. **If it goes wrong:** if the known-answer test fails, the arithmetic or the function is wrong. Read both before changing either. :::: ::: :::::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** let an agent snapshot, refactor and test working analysis code with one request, **trusted because** the reference came from the original code, committed by you before anything changed, and a shipped guard test checks that the agent's test reads it. - **Check:** the whole test suite; the diff in the Git pane; your own judgement of whether the unchanged output is right. - **Reproduce:** the suite passes after *Session → Restart R*, with nothing changed under `tests/fixtures/`. - **Record:** the committed reference, and your AI-log line: the request, whether the test passed first time, and what you changed. ::: ## Check your understanding **A characterisation test passes after a refactor. What has it established?**
**Why must the reference be captured and committed before the refactor starts?**
**The shipped deny rules protect tests/fixtures/ in Claude Code. Once you have committed the reference, which action could still change it?**
## Going further (not covered live) {#going-further} This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## What the skill does, step by step The skill turns a capture and two prompts into one request. By hand, you do the capture yourself: restart R, run `source(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R"))`, and commit the `.rds`. The two prompts are below. Splitting the work matters. A single prompt that writes both the refactor and the test lets one misunderstanding (about row order, say) shape both files at once. The result is a passing test that proves nothing. **Prompt 1: the refactor only.** ```text Move the computation in scripts/05_analysis.R into a documented function summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 05_analysis.R call the new function instead of the inline pipeline. Do not write any tests, and do not touch anything under tests/. ``` **Prompt 2: the test only.** ```text Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, read tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds, and compare it with summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) using expect_equal(). Do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/, and do not run tests/make_reference.R. I captured that reference myself; a reference you generate proves nothing. ``` Before you trust a passing test, check four things: 1. the test reads the `.rds` rather than hard-coding numbers; 2. it calls the function rather than reimplementing the pipeline; 3. nothing changed under `tests/fixtures/`; 4. the agent's commands (shown in the conversation) include no run of `tests/make_reference.R` after the capture you committed. The shipped `test_reference_guard.R` checks part of this automatically: that the test reads the `.rds` and calls the function, and that nothing under `tests/fixtures/` has changed since your commit. It cannot tell whether numbers were also typed into the test, or the pipeline copied into it. So read the test once yourself. The fourth check is why you read approval requests in Manual mode. :::{.callout-warning} **What a deny rule does not cover.** Claude Code's deny rules apply to its built-in file tools, to simple file commands it recognises (such as `cat`, `sed` and `tee`) and to shell redirects such as `> file`. They do not apply to R code or most other commands it runs ([Block 5](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)). The skill relies on that to take the first snapshot. But an agent that ran `Rscript tests/make_reference.R` again later would overwrite your reference without touching an edit tool. That is why git and `test_reference_guard.R` are the final checks. ::: To use the skill in your own projects, download it below. Unzip it into your project's `.agents/skills/`, and copy it into `.claude/skills/` for Claude Code: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: :::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Without an agent: write the function and the test yourself Here you write everything yourself; only `make_reference.R` and the data are shipped. First, capture and commit the reference as above. A tidy refactor naturally uses the modern `.by` argument. Write this first attempt in a new file, `scripts/functions/summary_functions.R`:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: first attempt ---- summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) } ``` :::
Now write the test and run it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_summary_functions.R ---- library(testthat) local_edition(3) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R")) test_that("summarise_metabolic_rate() reproduces the original summary", { reference <- readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds")) expect_equal(summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()), reference, tolerance = 1e-8) }) ``` ::: Run it as in Step 1: restart R, then run `testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))`.
It fails, and not on the numbers. `.by` returns the groups in order of first appearance. The reference, made with `group_by()`, has them sorted. The values are right but the rows are in a different order, so `expect_equal()` reports a mismatch. Add `dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)` to the end of the pipeline, and the test passes. That failure is the whole lesson on a small scale: a change that improved the code altered the output, and the characterisation test caught it. If your test passed first time, the data happen to be stored in sorted order. Check with `load_voles() |> dplyr::distinct(treatment_arm, sex)`.
Do not type the expected numbers into the test as literals. A test that compares the function with numbers you copied by hand proves nothing about whether the refactor kept the original computation. The test must *read the `.rds`*.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: refactored ---- #' Summarise post-treatment metabolic rate by treatment arm and sex #' #' @param data A data frame with columns treatment_arm, sex and #' metabolic_rate_post. #' @return A tibble with one row per treatment_arm and sex, sorted by both, #' giving the mean, standard deviation and number of rows. summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { stopifnot(is.data.frame(data)) required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post") missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data)) if (length(missing_cols) > 0) { stop( "`data` is missing required column(s): ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE ) } data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) |> dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/05_analysis.R: after refactoring ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "04_load_data.R")) source(here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R")) metabolic_summary <- summarise_metabolic_rate(voles) ``` :::
::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Protecting the new test by editing the settings file `/permissions` writes this same file when you choose the shared settings file. You can also add the rule by hand. Open `.claude/settings.json` in the editor and add `"Edit(/tests/test_summary_functions.R)"` to the `deny` list. Mind the comma after the line before. Claude Code reloads the file without a restart. Either way, commit the file, so the rule travels with the repository. `test_controls.R` checks that the rule is there. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## The review gate Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely. On GitHub, a pull request that changes a file under `tests/` can be held until the code owner reviews it. The self-study page [Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd) sets this up. ::: :::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Reuse the skill on a second step A skill pays off the second time you use it. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Reuse the skill (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** use the skill on a second step, with a reference you captured and committed yourself, so that you know its discipline holds on code it was not written for. **1. Capture a reference yourself first.** Pick a second step. It can be the plotting code in `scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R`, which you made in [Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd) (it is on `checkpoint-skills` if you need it), or a step from your own project. The skill runs only the shipped `make_reference.R`, so for any other step you do the capture yourself: - write a small capture script modelled on `make_reference.R` (for a plot, save `ggplot2::layer_data()` of it, as the [Copilot cloud-agent page](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd) does); - restart R, then run the script; - commit its output in `tests/fixtures/`; - protect the script with `/permissions` (choosing `.claude/settings.json`, as in Step 1). **2. Invoke the skill.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /characterisation-refactor Functionalise the step in scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R that I captured in tests/fixtures/. Start with the plan. ``` **3. Compare.** Did the agent still stop between the refactor and the test? Run the whole suite, and check the Git pane for anything changed under `tests/fixtures/`. **You are done when** the whole suite has no failures and the Git pane shows nothing changed under `tests/fixtures/` since you committed the new reference. :::: ::: To make a skill of your own from work like this, see *Turn a conversation into a skill* in [Block 4](11e-instructions-skills.qmd). ::::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## An asynchronous agent: the Copilot cloud agent The same discipline (your reference first, then a refactor, then a test, each reviewed) works with an agent that runs on GitHub while you do something else. The self-study page [Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd) applies it to the Block 3 plot script. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## The environment the test runs in A characterisation test is only as stable as the environment it runs in. The column types in `load_voles()` handle the finest-grained part. `renv.lock` pins the R version and package set. To run the tests on GitHub as well (`r-checks.yml`) and give a cloud agent the same packages (`copilot-setup-steps.yml`), see [Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd). ::: ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
characterisation test A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.
deny rule A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.
known-answer test A test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged.
reference In a characterisation test, the saved output of the original, trusted code (stored in tests/fixtures/). A trusted script captures it once, from the unchanged code, before any refactoring, and you commit it. After that, nothing regenerates it except your own recorded decision.
skill A reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.
````` ::: ::: ## References - GitHub documentation: *Configure the development environment* (Copilot cloud agent, `copilot-setup-steps.yml`), ; *About code owners*, . - r-lib/actions: *GitHub Actions for the R community*, .
